entity.name: Jacques Cartier
entity.description: The explorer who accidentally named Canada from a misunderstood word. A Breton mariner who made three voyages to the St. Lawrence River, Cartier mistook the Iroquoian word for village, kanata, as the name of an entire country. He kidnapped two chiefs' sons, survived scurvy thanks to Indigenous medicine, and brought back fake diamonds.

story.name: Jacques Cartier
story.description: Planting a cross at Gaspe to claim land for France, sailing upriver to Hochelaga, nearly dying of scurvy until the Iroquoians share a cure, then returning with fake diamonds. The accidental naming of Canada.

moments.name: Cartier Plants a 10-Metre Cross at Gaspe and Claims the Land for France
moments.subtitle: The Iroquoians clearly understand what the cross means and are not pleased
moments.description: On July 24, 1534, French explorer Jacques Cartier erected a 10-metre cross on the shores of Gaspe Bay bearing the words Long Live the King of France, claiming the territory for the French crown. A party of St. Lawrence Iroquoians watched as their land was claimed by a foreign power, and the change in their mood made clear they understood Cartier's actions. Cartier then kidnapped two sons of the Iroquoian chief Donnacona, promising to return them with European trade goods. This first voyage, commissioned by King Francis I to find a western passage to Asia, opened the St. Lawrence region to French colonization.

moments.name: Cartier Reaches Hochelaga and Is Blocked by Rapids He Mistakes for the Route to China
moments.subtitle: The rapids are named Lachine, French for China, because Cartier was so certain
moments.description: On October 2, 1535, Jacques Cartier sailed upriver from Stadacona (Quebec City) and arrived at the Iroquoian settlement of Hochelaga on Montreal Island, where over a thousand people greeted the French at the river's edge. Cartier could proceed no further because rapids blocked the river. So convinced was Cartier that the St. Lawrence was the Northwest Passage to China, the rapids and the town that later grew near them were named La Chine, French for China: the Lachine Rapids. This second voyage marked the first European navigation of the St. Lawrence River and the first recorded European contact with the site of modern Montreal.

moments.name: Cartier Learns a Scurvy Cure from the Iroquoians That Saves 85 Frenchmen
moments.subtitle: Only ten of 110 men were well enough to help the others before the remedy arrived
moments.description: During the brutal winter of 1535-1536, with Cartier's ships frozen solid at the mouth of the St. Charles River near Quebec, scurvy devastated both the Iroquoian and French populations. By mid-February, only ten of Cartier's 110 men were well enough to help the others. When Cartier noticed that the Iroquoian Domagaya had recovered from the disease, Domagaya revealed a remedy made from the bark of the annedda tree, likely white cedar. The Frenchmen consumed the bark of an entire tree in one week, and the treatment saved 85 men. This was one of the earliest recorded cases of Indigenous medical knowledge saving a European expedition.

moments.name: Cartier Returns to France with a Ship Full of Fake Diamonds and Fool's Gold
moments.subtitle: The haul of quartz and iron pyrites spawns a French proverb about Canadian diamonds
moments.description: In June 1542, Jacques Cartier abandoned his third Canadian expedition at Charlesbourg-Royal (present-day Cap-Rouge, Quebec) after Iroquoians killed about 35 settlers. Cartier sailed home to France carrying what he believed were diamonds and gold, but which proved to be quartz crystals and iron pyrites. The embarrassment gave rise to the French expression faux comme les diamants du Canada (as false as Canadian diamonds). When Cartier encountered his superior Roberval along the Newfoundland coast, he slipped away under cover of darkness rather than return to the colony. It was Cartier's last voyage; he died in Saint-Malo in 1557.

moments.name: Cartier Dies in Saint-Malo at Age 65 During an Epidemic
moments.subtitle: The man who named Canada never saw a permanent French settlement there
moments.description: On September 1, 1557, Jacques Cartier died in Saint-Malo at the age of 65, possibly of typhus during an epidemic. He was interred in Saint-Malo Cathedral. Despite three voyages to the St. Lawrence River between 1534 and 1542, no permanent European settlement would be established in Canada until 1605, nearly fifty years after Cartier's death. His most lasting legacy was unintentional: he applied the Iroquoian word kanata (village) to the entire territory, giving Canada its name. He was also the first European to map and describe the Gulf of Saint Lawrence and the river that became the highway of French colonization.
